summary: The MediaCtrl working group defined an architecture for controlling media services, with SIP used for signaling. Beyond what SIP routing offers, deployments need to choose a media server based on changing, application-level conditions. This document describes a Media Resource Broker that makes those choices, including in setups where many applications share many media servers.

eli5.summary: When many apps need a helper for audio or video, a receptionist picks which helper is free and suitable instead of every app guessing.

subtitle: A broker that matches applications to the media server best able to serve them, using published capacity and per-request needs.

tldr.problem: When many Application Servers can use many Media Servers with different capabilities and capacity, SIP routing alone cannot pick the most suitable media server for each request.
tldr.mechanism: A Media Resource Broker (MRB) collects capability and load reports from Media Servers over a Publish interface, and answers requests from Application Servers over a Consumer interface, either as a query over HTTP or in-line in SIP.
tldr.outcome: Application Servers get a leased reservation on suitable Media Servers, based on a best-effort view that the RFC says is approximate. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the status data show no later RFC replacing it.

facts.label: Suggested refresh point
facts.value: 80% of the timeout (240 s of 300 s)

today: RFC 6917 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2013, and the unit data show it has not been obsoleted or updated. The text itself does not describe any deployments, so nothing here claims who uses it.

sections.title: Why Brokering Is Needed
sections.content:
The IETF MediaCtrl working group defined an architecture where an Application Server controls a Media Server that does the audio and video work. SIP carries the signaling and already offers message routing. RFC 5167 and RFC 5567 state that it should be possible to have a many-to-many relationship between Application Servers and Media Servers.

The RFC walks through four deployment shapes: one Application Server and one Media Server; one Application Server with several Media Servers; several Application Servers with one Media Server; and the many-to-many case. Media Servers in a deployment may come from different vendors, and may differ in capability set, capacity or codec support.

Choosing among them needs more than static SIP routing. The new entity, the Media Resource Broker (MRB), collects information from Media Servers and selects resources on behalf of the applications that consume them. In the simplest single-Media-Server setup the RFC says an MRB is probably not required.

The RFC is explicit about limits. The MRB gives a best-effort view of resources at the time of the request, for the initial routing decision. How an MRB actually chooses a server, and how it learns things like planned downtime, is out of scope.
sections.eli5: If you have one helper, you just ask that helper. If you have a whole team with different skills, you want someone who knows who is free and who is good at what.

sections.title: Query and In-Line MRBs
sections.content:
The RFC describes two deployment models that share the same underlying mechanisms.

In the Query MRB model, Media Servers publish their capabilities and resources to the MRB. An Application Server asks the MRB for a suitable Media Server, then sends control commands and media dialogs straight to the one it was given. The MRB is not in the signaling path between the two.

The MRB can also be co-hosted. In a hybrid Query MRB it lives on the Application Server, which suits a single Application Server environment. It can instead be hosted on a Media Server, for example when one Media Server represents a pool of servers in a cluster.

In the In-Line MRB model there is no separate query. The Application Server sends its control channel and media dialog signaling to the MRB, which picks a Media Server and stays in the signaling path. An In-line MRB can act in one of two modes on a per-request basis:

  • In-line Aware MRB Mode (IAMM): the client knows about the MRB and states the characteristics it needs.
  • In-line Unaware MRB Mode (IUMM): the client knows nothing of the MRB, so the MRB must deduce the need from things such as SDP content, the requester's address, or Request-URI parameters per RFC 4240.

An MRB can run all three modes at once. It tells them apart by the request: an HTTP POST carrying application/mrb-consumer+xml is Query mode; a SIP INVITE with both that type and application/sdp is IAMM; a SIP INVITE with SDP but without the MRB type is IUMM.
sections.eli5: You can ask the receptionist who is free and then walk over yourself, or you can hand your request to the receptionist and let them connect you.

sections.title: The Publish Interface
sections.content:
Media Servers report to the MRB through the Publish interface, which is a Control Package for the Media Control Channel Framework (RFC 6230). The package is named mrb-publish/1.0, and any Media Server that wants to interact with an MRB MUST implement it.

The MRB subscribes. A <subscription> inside an <mrbrequest> has an id, a seqnumber that must keep increasing, and an action of create, update or remove. It may suggest <expires>, <minfrequency> and <maxfrequency> in seconds. The Media Server may change those values if it finds them unacceptable, and then must report the modified values in its response.

The Media Server then sends <mrbnotification> messages in CONTROL bodies. A notification MUST carry a <media-server-id> and a <media-server-status>, which is active, deactivated or unavailable. Optional elements include:

  • <supported-packages> and <supported-codecs> (with actions such as decoding, encoding and passthrough)
  • <active-rtp-sessions> and <non-active-rtp-sessions>, counting used and remaining RTP sessions per codec
  • <active-mixer-sessions> and <non-active-mixer-sessions>, for mixed sessions
  • <file-formats> and <application-data>

The numbers are described as approximate: the Media Server may give a best-effort computed view, and may report only periodically.
sections.eli5: Each helper keeps telling the receptionist what it can do and how busy it is, as often as the receptionist asked, so the list stays roughly up to date.

sections.title: The Consumer Interface and Leases
sections.content:
Application Servers use the Consumer interface to ask for resources. The request is a <mediaResourceRequest> with a client-generated id and three kinds of child: <generalInfo>, <ivrInfo> for interactive voice response needs, and <mixerInfo> for mixing needs. The answer is a <mediaResourceResponse> whose <response-session-info> lists one or more <media-server-address> elements, each with a SIP URI.

In Query mode the request travels in the body of an HTTP or HTTPS POST and the reply in the 200 response, always as application/mrb-consumer+xml. In IAMM the request is a SIP INVITE with a multipart/mixed body holding the SDP and the MRB XML. The MRB acts as a Back-to-Back User Agent, sends its own INVITE to the chosen Media Server, and returns a 200 OK with SDP plus the response XML. If it cannot reach any Media Server it MUST reply 503 with a non-zero Retry-After, and the Application Server MUST NOT retry before that time.

Granted resources are a lease. The response carries a <session-id>, a <seq> and an <expires> time in seconds. The client later sends the session id and an incremented seq with an action of update (which also works as a refresh) or remove. A new request carries no action. The RFC recommends a minimum lease of 300 seconds and refreshing at about 80 percent of it, which is 240 seconds in the example. The first seq SHOULD be random, not 1, and values stay within 0 to 2^31-1.

A B2BUA MRB changes the SIP dialog identifiers, which breaks the framework's connectionid. So it MUST include a <connection-id> element in the response, on exactly one media server address, and never in an HTTP response.
sections.eli5: The app tells the receptionist what it needs, gets a helper reserved for a while like a library book, and has to renew the loan or give it back.

sections.title: Status Codes
sections.content:
Both interfaces answer with a numeric status and a 200 means success. The Publish interface has its own codes, such as 401, 402 and 403 for a failed create, update or remove, 404 for a missing subscription, 405 for a wrong sequence number and 406 for an existing subscription.

The Consumer interface has seven codes, shown in the table. Wrong seq values cause a 405 and the request fails. A successful response MUST contain a <response-session-info>, and an unsuccessful one MUST NOT.

With IAMM over SIP, a failed INVITE does not advance the sequence. The Application Server MUST reuse the same seq value for its next request in that session.
sections.eli5: Every answer comes with a number that says whether it worked and, if not, roughly why, like a teacher marking a quiz.

sections.title: Choosing Between the Modes
sections.content:
The RFC compares five interaction types: Query, IAMM with a media dialog, IAMM with a Control Channel, IUMM with a media dialog and IUMM with a Control Channel. It says its observations are not exhaustive.

  • IUMM has no interface impact on an Application Server, so it helps legacy applications. The MRB just needs to be set as a SIP outbound proxy. It gives the least versatility, because the request lacks the resource description.
  • With IUMM and a Control Channel the MRB has even less information than with a media dialog, so a follow-up media dialog should go directly to the selected Media Server, not back through the MRB.
  • Query mode and IAMM with a Control Channel suit reserving a pool of resources in advance and changing the amount later. Query mode is decoupled from any Control Channel and usually needs fewer such channels over time.
  • For IUMM the RFC says the MRB should act as a SIP proxy rather than a B2BUA, so the Media Server URI reaches the Application Server and a direct dialog is possible.
sections.eli5: Some apps know how to talk to the receptionist and can ask for exactly what they want. Old apps just pick up the phone, so the receptionist has to guess what they need.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Both interfaces carry sensitive information. A malicious party on the Publish interface could change or delete subscriptions, or fake resource data so the MRB thinks nothing is available. The package inherits the security considerations of the Media Control Channel Framework.

On the Consumer side, a stolen or guessed session id would let an attacker shrink a session so media dialogs are rejected, or grow it to lock up the MRB's resources. The RFC strongly advises hard-to-guess session identifiers and a random starting sequence number. Over HTTP, bindings MUST be capable of running over TLS. Location data given by Media Servers should be used inside the selection logic and not passed on as is.

Neither interface has its own authentication. Any MRB-aware entity MUST support HTTP and SIP Digest authentication, although using it is optional. When an MRB acts as a B2BUA and changes bodies, SIP features that protect the body, such as RFC 4474, cannot be used unless the MRB mediates the security association.
sections.eli5: Because the receptionist's list decides who gets help, bad guys could lie to it or steal someone's reservation slip, so slips are hard to guess and conversations should be locked.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers the Media Control Channel Framework package mrb-publish/1.0, two media types, application/mrb-publish+xml and application/mrb-consumer+xml, plus URN sub-namespaces and XML schemas for both interfaces. The formal schemas for the Publish and Consumer interfaces are given in the RFC itself.
sections.eli5: It adds the new names to the official list so nobody else uses them for something different.

items.label: Syntax error
items.desc: Bad XML, schema violation or invalid value.

items.label: Wrong sequence number
items.desc: The seq value is not the expected increment.

items.label: Unable to find Resource
items.desc: No Media Server could meet the requirements.

items.label: Unable to update Resource
items.desc: The existing request could not be updated.

items.label: Unable to remove Resource
items.desc: The existing request could not be removed.

items.label: Unsupported attribute or element
items.desc: Request contains something the MRB does not understand.
